newsitem.title: UK: Bk of France aide doubts cenbank EMU gold sales.
newsitem.headline: Bk of France aide doubts cenbank EMU gold sales.

text.p: European central banks are unlikely to follow the example of Belgium in selling gold to build up their treasuries ahead of European Monetary Union (EMU), a Bank of France official said on Tuesday.
Alain Duchateau, head of the Bank of France foreign exchange and reserves management department, made his comments in remarks prepared for delivery at the Fifth Central Banking Conference in London.

"The operation carried out by the Belgian monetary authorities (between 1986 and 1996) was very specific and will probably not be imitated by other countries," he said. The Belgian sales were carried out so as not to affect the gold price.
But if several European countries were to start selling gold to improve their deficit figures in 1997 "the price of gold would be severely affected", Duchateau said.
"In addition, sales of gold would be one-off measures that would not allow any lasting deficit reduction," he said.
The impact would shake confidence in EMU and raise the spectre of economic crisis, Duchateau said.
The credibility of the European Central Bank (ECB) will depend heavily on the legacy of the national central banks.
As gold is the legacy of several centuries of central bank activity, it will remain an important reserve asset at national central bank level, he said.

"At the ECB itself, gold could be used to constitute part of the capital and part of the pooled foreign exchange reserves (equivalent to 50 billion Euro in gold and non EMU currencies," Duchateau said.
The share of gold in the reserves has not been decided but necessary gold movements between the national central banks and the ECB will be off-market and will not affect prices, he said.
